The article discusses two historical boxing matches, both significant for their political and cultural implications. The first is Floyd Mayweather vs Manny Pacquiao, expected to be financially and culturally impactful in the 21st century. The second, Joe Louis vs Max Schmeling, held in 1938, gained notoriety as a symbolic political war between America and Nazi Germany. Joe Louis, a high-profile campaigner for Civil Rights, avenged his earlier loss to Schmeling and was celebrated as a hero, while Schmeling, though later forcibly conscripted into the German army, became a hero in his own country following resistance to Hitler. Both Boxers remained friends until Louis's death in 1981, with Schmeling visiting him regularly at his Las Vegas job. This fight, the Fight Against the Nazis, is considered one of the most significant in boxing history due to its political and cultural implications.

The article discusses a new mobile game called None*, which is a text-based riddle game distributed on iOS, Android, and Windows Phone devices. The app is intentionally mysterious, offering only one clue for each level and no supporting images, music, animations, or hints. The game consists of 50 levels in its first episode, with clues that start with simple math problems and evolve to name associations, random statements, and coordinates. The game's creator, Dimitris Chassapakis, suggests that once players finish the first 50 levels, they can subscribe for the release of Episode 2, yet a small percentage of players have managed to complete the app. Reviews are varied, with some finding it fun and satisfying, while others find it frustrating for its vague clues and lack of context.

The upcoming GCSE changes in foreign language education for 14-16 year olds aim to make learning more contemporary and engaging by incorporating relatable topics such as tattoos, music festivals, YouTube, and rap music. Teenagers will be observed studying a review of a gritty foreign film, analyzing Spanish tweets about the Olympic Games, and discussingruntime topics like the Cannes Film Festival, volunteering abroad, and foreign cuisine. The focus is on enhancing students' linguistic abilities and enjoyment by incorporating grammar as a "toolkit" and employing fresh teaching methods inspired by English as a foreign language pedagogy.

A 21-year-old British woman named Danielle Davies gave birth to a 11lb 5oz baby named Harley after an eight-hour natural labor without any pain relief. The midwives were surprised due to the uncommon size, needing to weigh the baby numerous times for verification. Danielle, who previously had a 19-month-old daughter Layla, impressed hospital staff with her natural birth, despite having a blood clot on her brain just a month before, which required her pregnancy to be induced. A former midwife praised Danielle as a 'beacon,' highlighting her delivery of a big baby safely and easily.

The article discusses Linda and George Hunter, a couple who struggled to sell their home in Garrick Street, Liverpool, as the street underwent a regeneration scheme that led to neighboring houses being sold for £1. The Hunters, who became mortgage-free around 15 years ago and raised their four children in the house, now find their property's value significantly decreased due to the area's deterioration. An estate agent estimates their three-bedroom house is worth around £60,000, but selling it is highly unlikely due to nearby properties being offered for £1. The Hunters want the council to honor their original offer to move, feeling trapped and frustrated by the situation. Liverpool city council maintains that the £1 offer does not devalue other occupied houses in the area and that the regeneration scheme aims to revitalize the community.

Celebrities, such as Kim Kardashian, Myleene Klass, Mariah Carey, and Amanda Holden, celebrated Easter in typical family fashion, with activities like Easter egg hunts and baking treats. Kim Kardashian decorated Easter baskets for her daughter North West, among others. Mariah Carey baked Easter cupcakes for her twins Moroccan and Monroe. Myleene Klass held an Easter egg hunt with her daughters Ava and Hero. Amanda Holden and her daughters Hollie and Lexie embarked on their own Easter egg hunt. Other celebrities, like Fearne Cotton, Sam Bailey, Poppy Delevingne, and Lauren Laverne, also enjoyed a festive day, with some encountering unexpected Easter mishaps.

A convicted fraudster, Gabrielle Yinka Saunders, stole £17,000 from her latest employer, Insight Investments, where she worked as a personal assistant. The stolen funds were used to pay for her £10,000 wedding, a £5,000 honeymoon in the Seychelles, and other personal expenses. Despite having been convicted of fraud twice previously, Saunders was spared jail and instead was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment suspended for two years, with 200 hours of unpaid work, due to her repaying the money and her decision to retrain as a teacher.

A man, PJ Spraggins, lost 70lbs in a year to donate his kidney to his wife Tracy, who has been battling Lupus for over three decades and was on a seven-year waiting list for a transplant. However, his initial attempts to donate the kidney were foiled due to high blood pressure. Despite multiple setbacks, he embarked on a rigorous fitness regime to lower his blood pressure, and finally, in February 2015, they underwent the surgery at Vanderbilt hospital in Nashville. The transplant, described as a "festive Easter gift," was successful, with Tracy's kidney function now at 100%. The couple is now recuperating at home in Birmingham, Alabama, and is receiving financial support from friends during their two-month recovery period.

An animal lover, Pauline Kidner, is nursing orphaned badger cubs back to health after they were found by dogs in separate incidents. One of the cubs, named Little Star, was rescued just in time as it was carried away by a Jack Russell. The cubs were initially fed milk and have recently started eating custard creams to determine if they're ready for solid food. The cubs are doing well and growing rapidly. The aim is to release them back into the wild once they're strong enough after following a process that includes weaning, vaccination against Bovine TB, and transitioning them to nocturnal sleep before release.

Kimi Raikkonen, after a challenging 2014 season, feels that Ferrari has the potential to win the Formula One title this year, given their improved performance in the first three races compared to last season. Despite a qualifying issue that left him starting sixth at the Chinese Grand Prix, Raikkonen finished fourth in the race, reeling in teammate Sebastian Vettel and potentially challenging for a podium place. However, Raikkonen emphasizes the importance of improving his qualifying performance to boost his chances of title contention.

In his pursuit to strengthen Rangers' position in the playoffs, manager Stuart McCall aims for a win at Dumbarton on Saturday after a 1-1 draw against Livingston. Despite the points loss, McCall considers the draw as potentially crucial in the race for second place, with Rangers having only won once in their last five away matches. Livingston boss Mark Burchill expressed disappointment in his team's defense and missed opportunities, with a disallowed goal by Myles Hippolyte in the first half and a quick response by Rangers through Marius Zaliukas.

Nigel Farage, the Ukip leader, argues in a debate at the European Parliament that allowing refugees into Europe could provide a cover for Islamic extremists, potentially leading to millions of people from North Africa being given passports that could allow them to move to Britain. Farage plans to use this issue as a focus in the election campaign, hoping to create a "big shock" and thus gain more than ten MPs. If elected as MP for Thanet South, this could be Farage's last speech in the European Parliament. During a separate campaign visit, he accused the SNP of being "openly racist."

Kai Windsor, a 10-year-old boy, was born as a female but identified as a boy since age three. He shunned traditional girls' toys and started displaying boyish behavior at a young age. His mother Rachel, noticing these changes, supported him, and Kai is now set to undergo hormone treatment to halt puberty. The number of transgender referrals to the NHS for children under 11 has quadrupled since 2009, and Kai received supportive counseling and accommodations at his primary school to help him cope with his transition.

A Hawaiian fisherman, Ron Ingraham, is missing again, just months after surviving 12 days lost at sea. Previously, he had gotten caught in a storm on Thanksgiving, which left him adrift and surviving on raw fish. In the recent incident, his ship ran aground on rocks around a mile west of Hawaii's Lanai island. His sailing mate, Kenny Corder, was rescued and hospitalized. Ingraham was last seen clinging to a life ring before disappearing, and Coast Guard officials are still searching for him.

A father and son, Nicholas Pence and David Pence, were shot dead in an execution-style murder in their home in Metairie, Louisiana, following a celebratory football game in their garage. David, an oil company manager, was found dead sitting in an armchair, and Nicholas was found lying on the floor. The police have arrested 17-year-old Dexter Allen and 18-year-old Haraqyon Degruy, with Degruy being charged as an accessory to first-degree murder and Allen charged with two counts of first-degree murder. The community is shocked and mourning, with the victims being described as outgoing and good people. The investigation is ongoing, and it is unknown whether the alleged assailants had a link to the victims or a motive for the crime.

June Whitfield, known for her role as the eccentric grandmother in Absolutely Fabulous, is set to appear as Sister Ruth, a nun, in EastEnders next week. Her character will offer words of encouragement to Kat Moon, played by Jessie Wallace, who is struggling to deal with sexual abuse she suffered as a child. This marks Whitfield's recognition of the impressive standard of acting in EastEnders, following criticisms from actor Timothy West about the lack of value given to older characters and actors in soaps.

1. Lewis Hamilton maintains his position as the wealthiest athlete in Britain with a fortune of £88million, according to the 2015 Sunday Times Sport Rich List.
2. Wayne Rooney, Manchester United and England captain, has moved up into second place with a wealth of £72million, surpassing Jenson Button and rising £12million from last year's list.
3. Andy Murray takes the fourth spot on the list with wealth estimated at £48million, benefiting from endorsement deals with Standard Life and Under Armour.

Researchers at Yahoo Labs have developed a sensor technology named Bodyprint, which can identify users based on the unique shape and size of various body parts, such as ears, palms, or fingers. This technology turns a standard touchscreen into a biometric scanner, eliminating the need for specialized hardware like fingerprint readers or infrared cameras. The goal is to make unlocking devices more convenient and accessible. Tests have shown a high level of accuracy, with 99.98% accuracy in classifying body parts and 99.52% accuracy in user identification. However, a release date for this technology in consumer devices has not been announced yet.

A woman, Belinda from Essex, experienced regret after a Turkish surgeon's botched facelift left her with misplaced and visibly scarred ears. She initially sought the procedure to alleviate her 'worn out' appearance. The surgery, performed abroad to save money, resulted in scarring that dragged her earlobes down. Plastic surgeon consultant Vik Vijh later attempted to correct the damage, raising concerns about potential nerve damage and additional scarring. After the corrective surgery, Belinda reported feeling happier and more confident, her scars having drastically reduced. This incident will be featured in an upcoming episode of TLC's Extreme Beauty Disasters as a warning about the risks of cut-price surgery abroad.

In the article, Chuka Umunna, the shadow business secretary, accuses UKIP leader Nigel Farage of having a "problem with race," citing Farage's comments about "fully black" and "half black" UKIP supporters. This follows an incident where far-right supporters, including Gary Field, a former English Defence League organizer, were present at a UKIP event in South Thanet. Umunna alleges that UKIP has a virulent strain of racism within its party and criticizes the party for promoting anti-immigration sentiment. He emphasizes that he disagrees with blaming immigrants for societal problems, referencing his father's experience as a black immigrant in the UK during the 1960s and 1970s.

Model Maggie Rizer, 37, returned to her fit physique just nine weeks after giving birth to her third child, daughter Cecilia Kathryn. Despite facing admiration for her quick post-pregnancy transformation, Rizer thanked her Instagram followers for their kind comments and clarified that she posts her images carefully. Rizer, who is also a mother to two-year-old son Quinnlyn Clancy and three-year-old son Zander, is currently on a family vacation with her husband Alex Mehran at an undisclosed tropical destination, and continues to share her family's adventures on social media. Rizer was one of the world's most popular models in the late 90s and early 2000s but stopped modeling in 2004 due to financial mismanagement, with much of her earnings lost. Since then, she has been an advocate for AIDS awareness, following the death of her biological father from AIDS when she was 14.

Britons consume an average of four servings of cheese per week, with cheddar being the most popular variety. A significant portion of cheese lovers (26%) admit to eating melted cheese with everything, and three in ten office workers consume cheese sandwiches for lunch every workday. Food psychologist Greg Tucker suggests that repetitive eating habits can provide comfort and stability, but encouraging new tastes and experiences can stimulate and motivate individuals. Lurpak provides suggestions for alternate sandwich recipes, such as a chicken and mango sandwich with mint raita, a smoked ham and egg sandwich with capers, gherkins, and mustard mayo, and a vegetarian feta avocado and roasted red pepper sandwich.

A dress worn by Vivien Leigh as Scarlett O'Hara in the classic 1939 film Gone With the Wind fetched $137,000 at auction. This ensemble, initially slate blue-gray, has faded to light gray over the years, and was part of a collection of over 150 items from the film, offered at bid by Heritage Auctions. The dress was worn in key scenes, including encounters with Rhett Butler and an attack in the shanty town. Other top-selling items included a hat worn by Leigh, Gable's suit jacket and trousers, and a black bonnet worn by Leigh and Olivia DeHavilland. This auction occurred on the 75th anniversary of the film adaptation of Margaret Mitchell's 1936 novel, which follows a spoiled Old South socialite. Notably, Hattie McDaniel, who portrayed Scarlett's devoted nanny Mammy, became the first African-American actor to be nominated for and win an Academy Award.

A Turkish Airlines flight from Milan to Istanbul made an emergency landing at Ataturk Airport today due to its engine catching fire, marking the latest in a series of such incidents. The fire was extinguished, and all 97 passengers were safely evacuated without injuries. The right landing gear collapsed during the first landing attempt, causing the fire. This incident follows another emergency landing on March 30, due to a suspected bomb threat on a flight from Istanbul to Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Adam Leheup, a 34-year-old architect, was acquitted of rape and sexual assault by a jury at Blackfriars Crown Court. During a night-long date, Leheup and the 25-year-old woman involved in the incident had consumed wine and cocktails, with the woman allowing Leheup to remove her bra and massage her back with oil. Although the woman alleged that Leheup ignored her cries of "no" and penetrated her without her consent, the jury found Leheup not guilty. The woman claimed that Leheup had a habit of disregarding verbal "no" signals from women, but Leheup maintained during the trial that any sexual activity with the woman was consensual.

AleXsandro Palombo, an Italian artist and activist, has launched a photography campaign titled '#briefmessage' to combat gender violence. Women are writing their thoughts on machismo on their underwear and posting pictures on social media, encouraging men to join the fight against this issue.Palombo's project has sparked immediate and powerful reactions from participants, with messages ranging from defiant to simple, asserting women's rights and questioning the notion of men's strength. The artist emphasizes the importance of cultural and social education in overcoming gender violence, urging men to rebel against machismo and fight relentlessly against it.

Nick Clegg faced protests over his broken tuition fees pledge in Surbiton, South West London, where he also criticized George Osborne's "dangerous" economic plan. Clegg labeled Osborne as a "very dangerous man" and accused him of wanting to make drastic cuts that would harm public services. In contrast, Clegg described David Cameron as a "classic traditional shire Tory," whom he could tolerate. The Lib Dem leader stressed the need to prevent Osborne's proposed cuts and challenge the Labour Party's approach to public spending. Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Danny Alexander claimed that a senior Tory had told him in a private meeting that the Conservatives would prioritize tax cuts for the affluent while leaving working-class people to the Lib Dems.

Sharon Edwards, a 55-year-old teacher, has been missing since March 14 in Grafton, NSW. Her family is struggling to come to terms with her disappearance as her car was found in the driveway and her clothes were in the washing basket, but there was no sign of forced entry or any missed bank or social media activity. Police are treating the investigation as a homicide due to a lack of history of mental illness, but Edwards has no known enemies. The family is holding 'grave concerns' for her welfare, and police are asking for community assistance to find her. Edwards is described as Caucasian, fair-complexioned, short blond hair, and medium build. The investigation, Strike Force Burrow, is being led by detectives from the Coffs/Clarence Local Area Command and Northern Region.

A husband, Steven Nelms, authored a moving essay celebrating his stay-at-home wife, Glorianna, detailing the monetary value of her contributions to the family, including childcare, cleaning, cooking, grocery shopping, finance management, and laundry. He asserts that he can't afford to pay her the equivalent of a full-time nanny's salary for her work. He expressed regret over making his wife feel unappreciated by portraying her contributions as less valuable. The essay ends with Nelms expressing his deep appreciation for his wife, likening her value to that of precious jewels.

Prime Minister David Cameron is facing criticism for his election campaign's lackluster message and failure to pull ahead in the polls. In response, Cameron vowed to continue focusing on economic issues like jobs, business, and childcare. He emphasized the importance of a strong economy and argued that a stable government is necessary to achieve economic progress. Meanwhile, speculation persists about the possibility of Boris Johnson becoming the next Tory leader. Tory donor Peter Hall criticized Cameron's performance, stating that he lacks energy and conviction, and believes that Cameron's focus on economic management is not sufficient to win the election.

Two former police officials in Parma, Missouri, Trish Cohen and Rich Medley, have spoken out about their resignations following the election of the town's first black mayor, Tyus Byrd. They allege that their home addresses were shared online by Byrd's family members, causing them to fear for their safety. Byrd disputes these claims and denies knowing the reasons for the officials' resignations. Meanwhile, Byrd has stated she has never indicated she would interfere with the police department or publicly threatened to fire officers. Despite their public statements, neither Byrd nor Cohen responded to requests for comment.

Photographer Johan Bavman, inspired by Sweden's extensive parental leave policy, embarked on a project to document fathers taking advantage of the program. He encountered challenges in finding participating fathers but found dedication in those who did, capturing their genuine bond with their children. Bavman's aim was not to portray these men as superheroes, but as role models showing the challenges and rewards of parenthood, often leading to a reevaluation of their lives and potential career changes.

In Arizona, twins Eli and Silas Keslar, aged 18 months, tragically drowned in a canal after their mother was distracted by a bee and lost control of their stroller. Despite her desperate attempts to rescue them, the steep banks of the canal were too difficult to navigate, and the boys were swept away by the strong current. Authorities have warned of the deceptive nature of the canal's current and depth. A GoFundMe page has been set up to support the boys' parents, Mark and Alexis Keslar, which has already raised over $20,000.

Arsene Wenger is considering offering Abou Diaby, an injury-prone midfielder, a new contract, despite his extensive injury record at Arsenal. Diaby returned to action in a practice game on Wednesday, but his future at the club remains uncertain. Wenger also expressed his hope to extend the contracts of Tomas Rosicky and Mikel Arteta, both known for their injury struggles as well. Diaby has suffered a total of 42 injuries over his Arsenal career, with each injury occurring approximately every 79.5 days.

Eden Hazard, Chelsea's standout player this season, demonstrated his importance to their potential title victory by scoring a crucial first-half goal against Manchester United. He has significantly improved his finishing in the last 18 months, making him a key goal scorer for the team. Despite signs of fatigue, Chelsea is currently managing their league campaign effectively and looking likely to win the title. For Manchester United, despite controlling long periods of the game with their passing, they lacked the necessary punch, and Wayne Rooney's absence as a central striker affected their impetus in challenging matches.

In Panama City, President Obama had a historic handshake with Cuban leader Raul Castro at the Summit of the Americas, marking the first high-level meeting between the U.S. and Cuba in over 50 years. The conversation was about normalizing relations, with Obama expected to remove Cuba from the United States' list of countries that sponsor terrorism. The move is seen as a significant step towards rebuilding diplomatic ties, although some within the U.S. remain skeptical.

A mother, Latisha Fisher, has been charged with second-degree murder for allegedly smothering her 20-month-old son, Gavriel Ortiz-Fisher, in a bathroom at a Manhattan restaurant, claiming she did so to protect him from being eaten. Fisher has a history of psychiatric problems, including a previous diagnosis of schizophrenia, and was evaluated as mentally fit as recently as last year. Despite this, she was recommended for an alternative sentencing program after a 2011 stabbing incident. Witnesses reported that Fisher seemed emotionless after the incident, and her friends and neighbors have expressed concerns about her behavior and mental state in recent months.

The Star Wars: Episode VII - The Force Awakens panel was held at California's Anaheim Convention Center, missing Harrison Ford who was recovering from a plane crash. Carrie Fisher and Mark Hamill were present, thanking fans for their support over the decades. The second trailer for the movie was rolled out, and it was announced that Han Solo will be actively involved in the film. The trailer featured new faces like John Boyega and Daisy Ridley, as well as familiar characters like Chewbacca and R2D2. The trailer also hinted at the return of Darth Vader, and it was revealed that a new planet, Jaku, will be featured in the movie. The event was a gathering of Star Wars diehards, with Storm Troopers in attendance.

Bill Nye, also known as "the Science Guy", joined President Barack Obama on a trip to the Florida Everglades for an Earth Day excursion. Nye, who has a background in engineering, shared his love for jet fuel with the press before boarding Air Force One. The trip, a round trip of nearly 2,000 miles, raised questions about the carbon footprint due to jet travel. The president used the trip to promote his administration's commitment to reducing carbon pollution and preserving Florida's wetlands. The trip was met with criticism from Florida's Republican governor Rick Scott, who accused Obama and Congress of neglecting the Everglades and not providing adequate resources to protect it.

Floyd Mayweather Jr. reminisced about his friends' reactions when he announced his intention to establish his own boxing business in 2013, stating "The time will come when I make a hundred million dollars in one night." Critics called it a delayed move, but Mayweather argued it was all about timing. His upcoming fight against Manny Pacquiao on May 2, which is expected to generate more than $100 million for both fighters, serves as a testament to this strategy. As he prepared for the bout at his Las Vegas gym, surrounded by a significant media presence, Mayweather discussed aspects of the matchup, including his belief that Pacquiao might be affected by a neurosis about being the smaller fighter. Embracing his role as his own boss, Mayweather expressed that this fight represents the culmination of his career and legacy, although he plans to fulfill one more contractual obligation in a final fight at the MGM Grand in September.

The Elderflower Fields festival, a family-friendly event held at Pippingford Park in the Ashdown Forest, offers a blend of outdoor activities, live music, and luxury experiences for all ages. The festival is designed to stimulate children and families' interest in various areas such as sports, music, art, and the environment. Highlights include free activities for children like rafting, mud hut building, and sports camps, as well as cultural performances and workshops. The event also boasts a diverse range of musicians, including Danny and the Champions of the World, Patch and The Giant, and The Kings Parade. Additionally, there are the opportunity for spa treatments, camping, and picnicking, with ticket prices varying for adults and children.

Chelsea has won six spots in the Professional Footballers' Association Premier League Team of the Year. The defense includes John Terry, Gary Cahill, Branislav Ivanovic, and Ryan Bertrand, with Eden Hazard and Nemanja Matic in midfield and Diego Costa up front. Harry Kane of Tottenham is the only English attacking player, while Premier League players Philippe Coutinho, Alexis Sanchez, and David de Gea round out the team. Notably absent is Cesc Fabregas, who has provided more league assists than Coutinho this season.

Michael Owen, a 21-year-old father, was tragically killed in a car accident in Crowborough, East Sussex, while preparing for his daughter's fifth birthday. He had recently received a job offer in window screen repair. Kyle Careford, the other occupant of the car, is thought to have died just before his 21st birthday. The men were friends and local residents, and their loss has been mourned by family, friends, and community members. The accident occurred when their Renault Clio crashed into a church wall, leaving skid marks on the road and causing significant damage to the wall. The investigation into the cause of the collision is ongoing, and both men are expected to be formally identified the next day.

1. Manchester City fans have expressed a reserved attitude toward their team's potential as a European giant, with celebrity supporters like Ricky Hatton calling for a return to the club's earlier identity and Noel Gallagher noting apathy towards the Champions League.

2. Manager Manuel Pellegrini's position at Manchester City is under scrutiny after a series of losses, including a 4-1 defeat to their rivals, and critics argue that his calm demeanor is ill-suited for galvanizing the team during tough times.

3. Supporters and pundits criticize Manchester City for signing players like Jesus Navas who lack the quality to compete at the Champions League level and question their failure to pursue top talent like Cesc Fabregas, Diego Costa, and Angel di Maria, citing Financial Fair Play regulations as a limitation. They argue that Manchester City needs to think bigger and aim for a manager with true potential for greatness, such as Diego Simeone or Jurgen Klopp, to help the club reach its European ambitions.

A 39-year-old mother of two, Kim Callaghan, lost over ten stone after becoming concerned that her size was causing her to look masculine. Prior to her weight loss, Kim struggled to find clothes that suited her size 28 body and dressed in baggy, masculine clothing. After joining Slimming World in secret and adopting a healthier lifestyle, Kim has now slimmed down to a size 10 and feels confident and feminine. She no longer relies on catalogues for her wardrobe and enjoys shopping in regular stores. Kim's diet now consists of healthier meals like porridge, scrambled eggs, and chicken stir-fry, a drastic change from her previous diet of convenience foods like chicken kiev, deep-fried foods, and snacks.

Miami International Airport is currently experiencing an issue with baggage handlers excessively rummaging through passengers' bags, as part of an ongoing police investigation into luggage thefts. This issue is not exclusive to Miami, as a CNN analysis of a five-year period showed thefts of valuables from checked luggage at various airports, with John F. Kennedy International Airport having the most claims. Airports are taking steps to combat this issue, including setting up hidden cameras and increasing employee screenings, but thefts continue to occur.

Marla McCants, a woman who weighed 800 pounds, was on the brink of death due to her morbid obesity and refusal to move. After being discharged from the hospital due to her lack of cooperation, a desperate call from her daughter led weight loss expert Dr. Younan Nowzaradan to make a house call, convincing her to stand for the first time in years with the help of emergency medical technicians. This small victory gave Marla enough confidence to continue with her recovery, as she stood on a scale for the first time in five years and lost an estimated 266 pounds over the course of a year.

1. New findings from NASA's Mars rover Curiosity suggest there might be liquid water close to the surface of Mars, with the presence of perchlorate in the soil allowing for briny liquid water to exist.
2. Observations indicate that Gale Crater, where Curiosity is currently exploring, may have once been a large lake, with evidence of water erosion, old riverbeds, and sedimentary deposits found.
3. This discovery challenges previous beliefs that liquid water could not exist on the surface of Mars during its current ice age, and raises possibilities for future human habitation on the planet, but the radiation and cold climate make it unlikely for life as we know it on Earth to survive.

The article discusses the ongoing search for 11-year-old Luke Shambrook who went missing from a campsite in Victoria on Good Friday. Luke, who is autistic and known for hiding, was last seen at Candlebark Campground in Fraser National Park. Search efforts, which involve police, emergency crews, and volunteers, have been expanded to the Devils River area where he was reportedly seen. The police remain hopeful and positive about finding Luke, considering his high pain tolerance and the relatively favorable weather conditions. However, Luke's autism might make it challenging for him to respond to searchers. The search involves extensive combing of bushland and the banks of Lake Eildon, with over 200 other campers in the area during the busy Easter period potentially being able to spot Luke.

Nicola Sturgeon, the First Minister of Scotland, publicly expressed her support for immediately transferring all tax powers to the Scottish government, which could result in a £7.6 billion deficit in the country's finances. This proposal has drawn criticism from opposition parties, particularly Labour leader Jim Murphy, who warned it would have catastrophic consequences for Scotland's budget. Additionally, the SNP led by Sturgeon struggled during a TV election debate, with accusations of breaking promises, especially in regards to a potential second independence referendum.

The article discusses testimonies from victims who suffered abuse at the Neerkol orphanage in Australia, run by nuns and priests. Allegations include being raped with a broom handle, gang raped, and forced to drink their own urine. A woman, AYL, claimed she was routinely raped by a male employee from 1963, was later raped with a broom handle, and gave birth at a girls' home at 14, only for the child to be taken away. Another victim, AYB, stated she was raped over 100 times by priest Reginald Durham. The commission also heard from former nurse Mary Adams who suffered emotional, physical, and sexual mistreatment at the hands of nuns and priests at Neerkol. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sex Abuse in Rockhampton is investigating historical allegations of child abuse at the Neerkol orphanage, which operated from 1885 to 1978.

1. For the Kentucky Derby's 141st running on May 2 at Churchill Downs, selfie sticks are banned as a safety measure to protect horses and spectators on Derby Day, and live racing days at the venue.
2. The trend of banning selfie sticks is not limited to Churchill Downs, with other cultural institutions, music festivals, and sports venues around the world implementing similar policies due to safety concerns and potential disruption.
3. Institutions such as the Smithsonian, the National Gallery of Art, Coachella Music Festival, Lollapalooza Music Festival, various Premier League stadiums, and the Australian Open tennis tournament have already banned selfie sticks. These policies are aimed at ensuring patron and facility safety, while still encouraging selfies and social media engagement.

The Mercedes-Benz Fashion Week Australia concluded on Thursday with the Johanna Johnson show featuring Hollywood-inspired designs. Notable trends from the event included voluminous silhouettes, metallics, and sheer fabrics, while some concepts such as face bling, odd makeup looks, and bizarre headpieces were considered unconventional and not likely to be replicated in everyday wear. The week also featured contemporary designs, lazy, comfortable silhouettes, and a revival of Gladiator sandals. There were unique locations and sets for some shows, including Romance Was Born's Australiana-themed presentation in the Art Gallery of NSW and the Ten Pieces show at the iconic Icebergs pool. Notable incidents during the week included a neighbor complaining about the noise during Ellery's show and someone stealing tablets meant for front-row guests at Maticevski's show.

Prince William, 32, who recently started a new job as a pilot for East Anglian Air Ambulance, will take a two-week paternity leave when his second child is born later this month. After the birth, the Duchess of Cambridge, 33, will largely stay at their London home, Kensington Palace, before returning to the capital to recuperate and eventually give birth at the Lindo Wing of St Mary’s Hospital. Contingency plans are in place in case the Duchess goes into labor outside of London. The couple prefers to avoid a media frenzy surrounding the birth and will not announce the baby's arrival until at least 8am the next day if it happens after 10pm. The public and well-wishers are grateful and excited for the new addition to the royal family, who will be fourth in line to the throne.

A supermarket worker, Leanne Kenny, lost seven stone after consistently consuming end-of-the-day discounted junk food from her workplace. Struggling with her weight from childhood, Leanne gradually ballooned to nearly 20 stone and suffered from weight-related issues, including being unable to squeeze into the largest dress size in a store. The turning point came when Leanne broke down in a shop changing room due to not fitting into the largest dress. Motivated to change her lifestyle, she joined Weight Watchers, altered her diet, and took up walking. Leanne has since lost seven stone and aims to drop another dress size by the summer.

Ed Balls, the Shadow Chancellor, has been criticized for treating the public with contempt after dismissing the infamous Labour note about the nation's financial situation as a joke. The note, accidentally left behind by Liam Byrne in 2010, reads, "Dear Chief Secretary, I'm afraid there is no money. Kind regards – and good luck! Liam." The note became symbolic of Labour's fiscal irresponsibility and has been used by political opponents. Balls argued that the note was meant as a joke and insisted that Labour would reduce the deficit, with no additional borrowing needed. However, he was questioned about Labour's credibility regarding economic management. This has led to backlash, with Tories claiming Balls' remarks display a lack of understanding of the economic crisis and a disregard for the public. The letter has sparked controversy for years, becoming a tool for political opponents to highlight Labour's financial mismanagement.

1. The pursuit of journalists for paying public officials, in cases related to the 'Operation Elveden' probe, has been abandoned by prosecutors following a string of dropped cases, including the release of three Sun journalists and one former Daily Mirror reporter, as well as the overturning of a previous conviction.
2. The decision has sparked criticism toward the Crown Prosecution Service for still pursuing three Sun journalists for the same offenses, with many arguing that journalists should not be prosecuted for exposing matters of public interest.
3. The U-turn comes after the Court of Appeal criticized the application of the archaic law of misconduct in public office, leading to the overturning of several convictions and the dismissal of numerous cases. The move leaves the 'Operation Elveden' inquiry in disarray, with 23 of the 27 initially charged having been acquitted, cases dropped, or convictions overturned.

The District Attorney of Nashville, Tennessee, has banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization as part of plea deals, a practice that had occurred four times in the past five years. This practice has stirred public outrage, with some likening it to America's dark past of forcing sterilization on the mentally ill or "deficient." However, the use of sterilization in these cases involves a voluntary choice by the defendant as part of their punishment, rather than being linked to the eugenics movement or forced upon them. Critics argue that even if sterilization as a punishment is deemed cruel and unusual, it might still be constitutional if a defendant chooses it voluntarily, similar to how citizens can waive other constitutional rights. The outrage may stem from the gender bias that seems to have developed, as the idea of sterilizing male offenders, especially recidivist sexual predators and child molesters, is more acceptable to society than sterilizing female offenders.

A federal judge has sentenced former Blackwater security guard Nicholas Slatten to life in prison for his role in a 2007 shooting in Iraq that killed 14 civilians. Three other guards, Paul Slough, Evan Liberty, and Dustin Heard, received 30-year sentences for manslaughter, attempted manslaughter, and using firearms while committing a felony. The judge rejected both defense and prosecution motions regarding the sentences, considering the mandatory minimums appropriate, while acknowledging the stressful war-torn environment in which the guards operated. The victims and their families have testified about the horror and loss experienced on the day of the shootings, now a decade ago. The sentencing marks a significant point in the long legal fight over this incident, though further legal proceedings are inevitable.

In Mosul, Islamic State militants brutally beheaded four men accused of theft in a public execution, a punishment more severe than their usual penalty for theft. The men were reportedly interviewed by their captors before being executed, with crowds eagerly watching the execution. The U.S. has conducted airstrikes in Iraq and Syria against ISIS, with the Iraqi prime minister vowing to protect citizens and their rights once ISIS is driven out. In Tikrit, recently liberated from ISIS, Iraqi forces and Shiite militias have faced accusations of looting and vandalism in Sunni towns they have reclaimed.

Labour is currently divided over the proposal of a new 50p top rate of income tax, with Shadow Business Secretary Chuka Umunna advocating for it to be a temporary measure. This proposal contrasts with Ed Miliband's previous stance, where he expressed a more ideological commitment to maintaining the higher tax rate. Umunna argues that the decision to sustain the measure should be based on economic factors rather than moral ones. Additionally, Shadow Chancellor Ed Balls has suggested making the new top rate temporary, while Miliband has shown more resistance to this idea. Shadow Chancellor Ed Balls has also criticized the Conservative Party's manifesto, claiming it contains unexplained financial promises totaling £25 billion annually.

1. Bristol City secured promotion to the Championship after beating Bradford City 6-0, becoming the first team mathematically to secure promotion in the Football League this season. This season has been especially memorable, as the team also won the Johnstone's Paint Trophy at Wembley.

2. Central to Bristol City's success is defender Aden Flint, who led the team in scoring with 11 goals, many from set-pieces, and played a key role in their promotion. Flint expressed that he aims for the team to win the Championship, with the final game of the season left to secure this achievement.

3. Looking ahead, billionaire owner Steve Lansdown is funding a renovation of the club's Ashton Gate home to increase the capacity to 27,000 and make it Premier League-ready. Players and management express their ambition to take Bristol City even further, hoping to compete at the highest level and potentially make history by making the city of Bristol home to a Premier League team.

The article discusses the long-standing lack of recognition and awareness about the Armenian Genocide, which occurred during World War I and resulted in the deaths of over one million Armenians. The author notes that even famous Armenians, such as Cher, have had difficulty finding recognition for their Armenian heritage. The author also mentions the negative connotations that Armenians have faced due to their association with ending in "ian" and their portrayal in modern media. Recently, the Kardashian family's visit to Armenia brought attention to the genocide, with Kim Kardashian placing tulips at the Armenian Genocide memorial complex and dressing in red at one of her stops. This brought new color to a issue that is often remembered in funereal black. The article concludes by expressing hope that the attention brought by the Kardashians will help raise awareness about the Armenian Genocide and bring about a healing dialogue with Turkey.

The article discusses a Twitter post made by Janet Street-Porter, a British journalist, which jokingly compared a woman she met to Nicola Sturgeon, the First Minister of Scotland. The post sparked outrage from Sturgeon's supporters, who subjected Street-Porter to a wave of insults and threats. The article questions why Sturgeon, who is admired and idolized in Scotland, has become a figure who cannot be criticized, and compares the response to the intense defensiveness and distrust of English people among some SNP supporters. The author reflects on the tradition of political satire in the UK and speculates that Scotland may be becoming more like a repressive communist state, where the leader is not to be criticized. The article ends by questioning whether Sturgeon, a progressive party leader who has accepted significant donations from businesses that do not support equal rights for gays, is significantly different from other party leaders in the UK.

The article discusses England football supporters singing anti-IRA songs during a friendly match with Italy in Turin, which has been a recurring issue in the team's overseas trips. The songs, such as 'Where were you in World War Two,' and the German bomber song, have been seen as embarrassing and potentially provocative, particularly in Ireland. The FA is caught in a difficult position, dealing with fan behavior and addressing concerns about antiquated songs that many younger fans may not understand. The article also touches upon the England fans' dissatisfaction with the FA's loyalty scheme for travel rewards, which has led to criticism and unrest among supporters.

Arkansas Republican Governor Asa Hutchinson has decided not to sign a controversial religious freedom bill, citing influence from his politically liberal son Seth, who had signed a petition asking him to veto it. The governor's concerns revolve around the bill not aligning with the 1993 federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act, being potentially discriminatory and going beyond the protections provided by the federal law. Seth, who works as a labor organizing coordinator in Texas, expressed his opposition to the bill despite his love for the state of Arkansas and hope that a groundswell of grassroots opposition will drive change. The White House has expressed support for Hutchinson's decision, with press secretary Josh Earnest stating that such laws could be used to justify discrimination against individuals based on their sexual orientation.

Hillary Clinton has announced her candidacy for the 2016 presidential election, making her a barometer for gender equality in the USA. If she wins, it signifies a significant step towards women's political inclusion, but persistent issues like pay inequities, sexual assault, and human trafficking will persist. If Clinton loses, it might perpetuate the notion that women can't win big elections, making it harder for future female candidates. However, Clinton's candidacy should not be the sole measure of gender equality as political landscape and partisanship largely drive election outcomes.

The Clinton Foundation, with Hillary Clinton running for president, will continue to accept donations from six foreign governments while limiting donor nations, effectively ending contributions from 10 other governments due to concerns over human rights abuses and potential conflicts of interest. The charity will increase transparency by disclosing donors every quarter rather than annually, and will stop holding CGI meetings abroad. The six governments that will continue to donate are considered low-risk due to their uncontroversial ties with the U.S. However, one of the six governments, Canada, has advocated for the Keystone XL pipeline, a controversial project in the U.S. climate change debate. The Clinton Foundation claims it is not involved in the Keystone XL issue and has a program aimed at reducing carbon emissions.

1. Many popular brands are reducing the size of their products, such as Cadbury's Fingers, Creme Eggs, PG Tips teabags, and John West tuna, to cut production costs. These reductions in size often occur without corresponding price reductions, leading consumers to feel they are being short-changed.

2. This practice, known as 'shrinkflation,' is a common strategy among retailers to increase profits without raising the price of products, potentially causing consumer anger and frustration.

3. While companies may argue that reductions in product size are partially motivated by efforts to support public health via weight loss, confectionery industry analysts dispute this claim, asserting that smaller product sizes often lead to consumers purchasing and consuming more.

On St George's Day, April 23, patriotic citizens across England celebrated with parades, Morris dancing, and flag-waving. Notable events included the annual Nottingham St George's Day Parade, the 12th Regiment Royal Artillery parade in Emsworth, and the Leadenhall Market display in the City of London. The day was characterized by warm temperatures, with parts of the country reaching up to 20C. The festivities aimed to celebrate England's cultural heritage, including contributions in arts, industries, and the world stage. A drop in temperatures is expected over the weekend, following a week of unusually warm weather.

Manchester City recovered from their recent derby loss by defeating West Ham 2-0, with Sergio Aguero scoring the decisive goal. The team's performances were rated in the game, with Jesus Navas receiving high praise for his improved performance on the right. West Ham's defense was criticized, with Central defender James Collins realizing a freak own-goal early in the match. Notable players include City's Frank Lampard, who showed signs of lack match sharpness and West Ham's Enner Valencia, who was more productive in the second half, but overall anonymous.

Andy Murray and his fiancee Kim Sears are set to marry this weekend in Dunblane, Scotland, modeled after the decorations at Prince William and Kate Middleton's wedding. Trees have been spotted being delivered to the cathedral ahead of the ceremony. The town has been embracing the celebration with bunting and special-themed produce in many of the stores. Local businesses, including Point Nouveau Bridal shop, have sent gifts to the couple in advance of their big day.

Inhabitants of Dunblane have been preparing for the wedding of their famous resident, with messages and mascots featured in store windows. Murray's uncle, Niall Erskine, suggests the decision to hold the ceremony at the cathedral, rather than at Murray's hotel, Cromlix House, was made to allow the community to also toast the big day.

Despite being one of the world's top tennis players, Murray's guests for the wedding include close family and friends, with only a few notable figures from the tennis world expected to attend.

Andy Murray, scheduled to marry next weekend, lost to Novak Djokovic in the Miami Open final in straight sets after a challenging match under harsh sunlight. In the first set, Murray exhibit strong play but struggled serving into the sun, with both players breaking serve multiple times. The second set was more even, with Murray growing increasingly frustrated as he failed to secure the break. Djokovic grew angry as well, taking his towel from a ballboy and screaming at his box. Despite a strong second set, Murray struggled in the third set, losing 6-0 to Djokovic. Murray has now lost ten out of eleven matches against Djokovic, raising questions about how to beat this formidable competitor. After the match, Murray expressed frustration about his inability to win against Djokovic and his struggles in the third set.

A New Zealand couple, Justin and Jola, transformed a large truck into a unique, castle-like home for their family, complete with a rooftop bathtub. The house, which includes a kitchen, lounge, and bedroom in a compact structure, is used for their travelling lifestyle due to Jola's job as an acrobat. The interior features handmade furniture made from recycled materials, a composting toilet, and a shower and washing machine. The truck's design allows it to meet minimum road requirements when in travel mode, and the family continues to make modifications and improvements to their mobile home.

A 26-year-old woman named Elizabeth Elena Laguna Salgado, originally from Chiapas, Mexico, has been missing for a week after disappearing in Provo, Utah. She was last seen leaving a language school on April 16 and has not made contact with anyone since. Elizabeth Smart and her father have joined the effort to find Salgado, with Smart citing the importance of public awareness leading to her own rescue after being kidnapped in 2002. The Provo Police Department is investigating possible leads, and Salgado's loved ones have started a Facebook page to share information and raise awareness about her disappearance.

World heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko is preparing for a title defense against American challenger Bryant Jennings, but his thoughts remain on the ongoing conflict in Ukraine. He expressed shock and upset over the crisis in his homeland, stating that it has left him feeling as though Ukrainians and Russians are being divided by war, with Russia being a source of aggression instead of Ukraine. Klitschko has been a prominent figure in Ukrainian politics, and is hopeful that with international support, Ukraine can forge a democratic future. He remains active in the country when his boxing schedule allows, and recently welcomed a new daughter with his fiancée, actress Hayden Panettiere. Klitschko is unsure of when he will retire from boxing, but is eager to continue fighting for peace and a better future for Ukraine outside the ring.

A 21-year-old woman named Jamyra Gallmon, who attended a military academy, has been charged with the murder of David Messerschmitt, a married lawyer, in an upscale DC hotel. The killing occurred on February 9, and Messerschmitt was found dead with multiple stab wounds and various items such as a computer, lubricant, condoms, and cell phone in his hotel room. Police sources, citing surveillance footage, have identified Gallmon as the woman seen entering the hotel that evening, allegedly for a sexual encounter that they believe may have motived the robbery. Gallmon's mother stated that her daughter had never been in trouble before and had an ambition to join the military.

The article discusses the controversial views of a female businesswoman, Cheryl Rios, who believes a woman's hormones make them unsuitable for presidency due to the potential for irrational decisions leading to unnecessary wars. However, the article raises concerns that such beliefs reveal ingrained gender bias, particularly in the workplace. Research suggests that women tend to take fewer risks than men and are less likely to engage in unethical behavior. Rios, while facing criticism for her views, is not alone in challenging the idea that a woman's hormones could negatively impact leadership. The article highlights the pervasive gender bias, which not only hinders women's potential but also undermines overall equality, economic growth, and family dynamics.

A mother named Valerie Cadman-Khan has successfully sued Cleveland Police for wrongful arrest after being handcuffed in front of her 12-year-old daughter with Down syndrome. Despite winning the lawsuit, she hasn't received an apology from the police. The incident occurred in 2008 when Detective Sergeant Colin Helyer arrested Valerie, alleging child neglect, based on false claims that Aimee had been left alone for 45 minutes in the cold. During the trial, it was revealed that Helyer had lied under oath about the events, leading to Valerie's arrest. Following the verdict, Cleveland Police has promised to apologize once the judge determines the suitable reward for Valerie.

A victim, Richard Kerr, has claimed that he and other vulnerable boys from a children's home in Belfast were trafficked to London in the 1970s, where they were allegedly abused by powerful figures including politicians, members of the royal household, and Cabinet ministers at known locations like Dolphin Square and Elm Guest House. The allegations are now under investigation by Scotland Yard. Richard Kerr's story provides a link between three alleged major VIP paedophile rings that operated in London and Northern Ireland. His account also sheds light on the alleged cover-up at Kincora children's home in Belfast, where MI5 is accused of blocking police investigations into abuse.

A California parole board has granted parole to James Schoenfeld, one of three kidnappers who abducted 26 school children in 1976, inspired by the film Dirty Harry. Schoenfeld spent 39 years in prison after keeping the children 'buried alive' in an underground trailer while negotiating a $5 million ransom. The parole decision will undergo a four-month internal review before a recommended parole date is sent to Governor Jerry Brown. The victims of the kidnapping, including Jennifer Brown Hyde who was 9-years-old during the incident, expressed their desire for their captors to remain in jail and described the lifelong trauma they have endured.

California Governor Jerry Brown has ordered a 25% reduction in water use by cities and towns due to the ongoing drought. The reduction applies to residents, industrial and recreational facilities, and businesses, with the aim to conserve water amidst California's fourth summer of drought. State reservoirs have a year's worth of water but the low snowfall over the winter means little replenishment. Some wells in parts of the state are already going dry as groundwater levels fall. The water agencies have been mandated to reduce water use by one-quarter from the 2013 level. The state government will offer rebates for replacing water-thirsty lawns with drought-resistant plants and for installing water-efficient appliances and plumbing fixtures. The new regulations are expected to affect cemeteries, golf courses, and businesses, with significant cuts in watering grass and shrubs, and new homes being prohibited from using drinking water for irrigation unless they have water-saving drip systems. However, enforcement details have yet to be substantially worked out, and some experts question the success of the water conservation campaign, noting that agriculture, which consumes 80%

Charlotte Cosby, a 24-year-old reality TV star, has faced criticism for appearing unusually thin after losing over two and a half stone in the last year. Some fans have expressed concern that she has taken drastic measures to achieve this figure, while others have voiced their approval. Fellow Geordie Shore stars Vicky Pattison, Holly Hagan, and Marnie Simpson have also lost weight over the past year. They have attributed their weight loss to exercise and a healthier diet. However, one doctor has suggested that the pressure to maintain a slim figure in the media can lead to unhealthy eating patterns and potential health problems. Holly Hagan and Charlotte Crosby have dismissed such criticism, arguing that their weight loss is not as rapid or extreme as it may appear in media reports.

The #ThisDoesn'tMeanYes campaign in London aims to address the persistent myth that a woman's clothing choices can imply consent to rape. The initiative, led by Rape Crisis London and photographer Perou, features over 2,000 photographs of 200 women in various outfits to demonstrate that clothing is not a form of consent, and the responsibility for rape lies solely with the attacker. The campaign urges women to join by uploading their photos on Instagram with the hashtag #ThisDoesn'tMeanYes, as part of the ongoing effort to challenge victim blaming in rape cases. Recent statistics show that a significant minority, particularly among the younger generation, still hold the belief that victims are partially responsible if they are drunk at the time of the attack.

An aspiring model, Leonie Granger, was convicted of manslaughter for luring a professional gambler, Mehmet Hassan, leading to his death. She befriended him, received gifts, cash, and was seen laughing with two accomplices in footage retrieve from her mobile phone. The jury cleared Granger of murder but found her guilty of Mr Hassan's manslaughter. Her boyfriend, Kyrron Jackson, and another accomplice, Nicholas Chandler, were convicted of murder, robbery, false imprisonment, and firearms offenses. The gang had previously held up a South Kensington casino at gunpoint. Granger, who worked as a care worker for elderly dementia patients, was found guilty by a majority of 10 to 2. Mr Hassan's family expressed their ongoing grief and love for him. All three will be sentenced on April 28.

The Tory government plans to force thousands of children who fail elementary maths and English tests at age 11 to re-sit them in their first year of secondary school. This measure aims to ensure children can read, write, and perform basic arithmetic. The Prime Minister, David Cameron, believes these changes will aid in a child's success in future education and improve the nation's competitiveness globally. This policy, set to begin in 2016 if the Tories win the election, is intended to address the issue that one in five children do not meet the expected standard in English and maths at the age of 11. Critics, such as the Labour's education spokesman Tristram Hunt, argue that this policy is a desperate attempt to cover up the Tories' failures in school standards.

The article discusses the return of Jonathan Trott to international cricket after a 18-month absence due to mental health issues, his impressive performance scoring 72 runs in a practice match against St Kitts and Nevis Invitational XI. Alastair Cook, who is captaining the England team, also performed well, posting an unbeaten 95. Both Trott and Cook came together as opening batsmen, a move first attempted five years ago in Bangladesh. England's World Cup exit in 2015 led to scrutiny, and the article notes that the team is still on trial despite ending the 2015 Test summer with three wins against India. The return of Ben Stokes and the poor performance of St Kitts Invitational XI were also mentioned. The article speculates on the potential role of Stokes, Chris Jordan, Mark Wood, Liam Plunkett, Adil Rashid, and James Tredwell in upcoming tests.

Labour announced a series of policies aimed at helping first-time home buyers, including the abolition of stamp duty for homes under £300,000, prioritizing new homes for local people, and rent control measures. The policies, particularly the ban on landbanking, have led to a drop in the value of shares in leading housebuilding firms, with Barrett Developments, Taylor Wimpey, and Persimmon seeing declines in their share prices. The move to clamp down on landbanking has been unpopular with developers, as it could affect their profits by forcing them to build on undeveloped sites more quickly. Labour also plans to introduce higher taxes on foreign buyers, create a national register of landlords, and reduce tax relief for landlords renting out sub-standard properties. Other parties, such as the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats, have criticized Labour's proposals as unfunded and unrealistic.

George W. Bush criticized Barack Obama's foreign policy at a private meeting with Jewish donors in Las Vegas, expressing concerns about the planned lifting of sanctions on Iran. He argued that the deal could weaken America's negotiating power, claiming Iran's government was already caving in, and suggested the nuclear deal would negatively impact US national security. Bush also criticized Obama for not having a clear strategy to defeat ISIS, stating that when a president makes promises, they should be followed through. Additionally, Bush commented on the 2016 presidential campaign, suggesting that his brother, Jeb Bush, might face difficulties due to the American aversion to political dynasties.

Edward Ronayne, a husband from Liverpool, was awarded £9,000 in compensation for experiencing nervous shock due to his wife's disfiguring post-surgery appearance, despite her already receiving a large settlement. The case, which could establish a significant precedent, involves a botched hysterectomy in 2008 that left Julie Ronayneappearing like the Michelin Man due to peritonitis. The NHS is challenging the payout, fearing financial repercussions. In the appeal court hearing, it was argued that Mr. Ronayne's claim expands the scope of nervous shock victims, potentially leading to a wave of similar claims. The judges have reserved their decision on the NHS's appeal.

Bruce Jenner, the former Olympic gold medalist, is set to premiere an eight-episode docu-series on July 27 that will chronicle his transition into a woman. His adult children, Burt, Brandon, Brody Jenner, and stepdaughter Kim Kardashian, are expressing concern about him revealing too much of his journey on reality TV, suggesting he should finish the process in private. Despite their reservations, Jenner's children have expressed pride in him, with some even calling him a hero. The children are worried that the docu-series might "de-class" what Jenner has accomplished, and they have urged him not to do other interviews.

1. Mark Wood, a 25-year-old Durham paceman, has been called up by England for the Test series against West Indies. Despite his unconventional size for a fast bowler, he is renowned for his speed and ability to swing the ball, particularly reverse swing.

2. Wood has demonstrated significant improvements in his use of the new ball, which he showcased during the 2014 season. He has also been able to maintain his fitness, playing a series of matches following a career marred by injuries.

3. Despite the pressure, Wood remains confident and aims to emulate the success of fellow Geordie and former England fast bowler Steve Harmison, who earned the nickname "Grievous Bodily Harmison" for his performance at Sabina Park in 2007. He is preparing to bring his unique strategies, such as using an imaginary horse to keep things interesting during long fielding stints, to the West Indies series.

A woman named Dawn Williamson, who had a 30-year-long phobia of snakes, was cured live on TV in an astonishing ten minutes. Her intense fear originated from a B-movie she watched at age seven. Therapists Nik and Eva Speakman broke down Dawn's phobia by demonstrating its irrationality and helping her confront her fear. By the end of the show, Dawn was able to touch and even stroke a 9ft Burmese python, leaving both hosts and viewers amazed. the Speakmans have helped 60 individuals overcome their fears and phobias through similar methods on TV, with Dawn being the 60th case.

Apple has acquired LinX, an Israeli company that produces 'multi-aperture' cameras with depth-sensing technology, for approximately $20 million (£13.5 million). This technology, which is small enough to fit into smartphones and tablets, allows for post-capture refocusing of images and measuring the dimensions of a room. The technology being used by LinX could potentially be integrated into the next-generation iPhones and iPads. The technology used by LinX combines multiple sensors to provide an image with a greater depth of field, as seen in the HTC One M8's Duo Camera. Apple has not released any further details regarding its plans for the newly acquired technology.

Chris Ramsey, QPR's interim manager, has expressed his long-term commitment to the club, stating he will remain as long as they want him, regardless of the division they are in next season. He aims to contribute to the development of the club's academy and build a lasting project. Despite speculation about potential job offers, including a possible collaboration with Tim Sherwood at Aston Villa, Ramsey is focused solely on QPR. He highlights the club's loyalty towards him in the past and expresses a desire to return the favor by showing loyalty towards QPR. The final decision on the next manager rests with QPR owner Tony Fernandes. Ramsey acknowledges Les Ferdinand's role in the club's improvement and believes Ferdinand will become a top figure in his field. Ramsey harbors ambitions of becoming a top manager himself and is keen to secure a permanent management position, preferably at QPR.

The son of Brunei's Sultan, Prince Abdul Malik, has married Dayangku Raabi'atul 'Adawiyyah Pengiran Haji Bolkiah in an opulent ceremony held at the Sultan's 1,788-room palace, Istana Nural Iman, in Brunei. The ceremony was attended by various foreign dignitaries, and featured the couple adorned in matching gold outfits, embellished with diamonds, and Raabi'atul carrying a bouquet made of dazzling gems. The prince is second in line to become the next Sultan of Brunei. The wedding, which took place over 11 days, saw elaborate ceremonies, and the couple later changed into more opulent evening outfits for the wedding banquet.

Matilda Kahl, an art director at Saatchi & Saatchi, wears the same work 'uniform' every day – black trousers, white shirt, and a custom rosette – to eliminate the stress of deciding what to wear and to be judged on her work rather than her appearance. After feeling uncomfortable at a meeting when her male colleagues looked more relaxed in their attire, she decided to simplify her morning routine by wearing the same outfit every day, and finds comfort and creative freedom in her uniform. Despite facing some criticism, Matilda continues to wear her uniform and asserts that it has saved her time, money, and has given her a new sense of control.

A toddler was left hanging by her neck after crawling out of a cot with a gaps in the handrail. Her mother was alerted to the incident through a baby monitor and rushed upstairs to save her. The supplier of the cot, furniture boss Phillip Dickens, was fined £50,000 and given a suspended prison sentence for placing an unsafe product on the market. In another incident, a second toddler was found dangling from the same cotbed. Both incidents occurred due to the design of the cot, which was found to not comply with British safety standards. The manufacturer, Baumhaus Ltd, was fined £12,000 and faced prosecution costs of £35,653. The judge suspended Dickens' jail sentence due to lack of intent to cause injury. The mother of the saved toddler urged every parent to consider a video monitor for their child. Trading Standards Officer Rebecca Kaya emphasized the need for caution when buying online and for having manufacturer's codes, product codes, and full contact details of the retailer before purchasing a product.

1. The Moai statues of Easter Island, ranging up to 40ft tall and adorned with distinctive 'hats' of red stone, have puzzled experts for centuries.

2. A team of researchers, including Sean Hixon from the University of Oregon, now believe they have solved the mystery of how the Rapa Nui people placed these red stone 'pukao' on the figures' heads, over 700 years ago. They suggest the stones were likely rolled up ramps.

3. Despite their size, the team believes a relatively small number of people could have accomplished this task, either by levering or rolling. However, the largest pukaos measure six-and-a-half feet in diameter and the heaviest weigh 12 tonnes.

The shadow chancellor, Ed Balls, has hinted at a potential increase in the corporation tax rate if Labour forms the next government, a move that concerned businesses and critics. He was evasive about the 40p rate of income tax and committed only to keeping the main rate 'the lowest in the G7.' Additionally, the Conservative party pledged to sell off billions of pounds of shares in Lloyds Bank to the public at a discount rate within a year.

The Salt card is a new device intended to simplify smartphone unlocking by using Bluetooth technology to automatically unlock devices when the user is within 10 feet, and lock them again when they move out of range. Created by Joel Paglione and Niko Zistakis, the card is designed to save users around 53 hours per year. It also sends notifications if the user strays too far from their wallet, where it is suggested the card is stored. The card costs $20 and is made of durable plastic with a matte finish, slightly thicker due to integrating a battery that lasts for 18 months. The inventors claim it is more secure than fingerprint scanners, as it works with gloves and on wet or dirty hands. While there are similar products, the Salt card is unique as it is a compact, affordable device that can be hidden away. The inventors hope to expand the card's functionality to include communicating with various electronic devices in the future.

In a crucial Championship game, Middlesbrough defeated Wolves with goals from Jelle Vossen and Patrick Bamford, boosting their chances of promotion to the Premier League. Bamford, on loan from Chelsea, showcased his talent and was named Man of the Match, with 17 league goals this season, a record for a Middlesbrough player in 25 years. The victory leaves Middlesbrough with three remaining games, including a trip to Norwich, to secure automatic promotion.
